about.title: Geometric Sequences and Linear vs Exponential
about.length_note: This class has two linked ideas: writing a geometric rule, then telling linear from exponential. I split it into 22 short steps with a check after each idea. That makes it about 35 minutes, a little over 30. You can pause after step 12 and finish the rest another day.

Comparing Linear and Exponential Functions (Math 1, Lesson 6.4)

say.text: Hi, {name}. Today we sort growth into two kinds: the kind that adds, and the kind that multiplies.
Picture a game that pays coins each level. Deal A: 10 coins per level. Deal B: 1 coin, then it doubles every level. Hold that thought.
First, a quick reminder. Deal A adds the same amount each step: 10, 20, 30, 40. That is the adding kind.
The multiplying kind is a geometric sequence. Each term is the one before it times the same number.
That repeated number is the common ratio. To find it, divide any term by the term before it.

show.text: Common ratio r: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so r = 2

say.text: Your turn. Divide each term by the one before it.

ask.q: What is the common ratio of 5, 15, 45, 135?

say.text: The ratio can be smaller than 1. Then the terms shrink. 80, 40, 20, 10 has ratio 1/2, since 40 ÷ 80 = 0.5.

ask.q: What is the common ratio of 100, 50, 25?
ask.why: 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5, and 25 ÷ 50 = 0.5. The terms get cut in half each step.

say.text: Once you know the ratio, you can build the sequence. Start with the first term and multiply by r again and again.

ask.q: A geometric sequence starts 2, 6, 18. What is the next term?
ask.why: The ratio is 3, so 18 × 3 = 54. The answer 24 would come from adding 6, which is the adding kind.

say.text: Counting up one term at a time is slow if you want term 50. So we use an explicit rule. It jumps straight to any term.
Why n minus 1? Term 1 has no multiplying. Term 2 is multiplied once. Term 3 is multiplied twice. Term n is multiplied n minus 1 times.

show.text:
Term 1: a₁
Term 2: a₁ · r
Term 3: a₁ · r · r
Term n: a₁ · r^(n−1)

say.text: Example: 2, 10, 50, 250. The ratio is 10 ÷ 2 = 5, and the first term is 2. So the rule is aₙ = 2 · 5^(n−1).

show.text: First term a₁ = 2 | Ratio r = 5 | Rule: aₙ = 2 · 5^(n−1) | 5th term: 2 · 5⁴ = 2 · 625 = 1250

say.text: Now use a rule. Put the term number in for n. Do the power first, then multiply.

ask.q: For aₙ = 5 · 2^(n−1), what is the 6th term?
ask.why: For n = 6 the power is 2⁵ = 32, and 5 × 32 = 160. 320 comes from using 2⁶, which forgets the minus 1.

say.text: Now go the other way: write the rule yourself. Find the first term, then the ratio.

ask.why: The first term is 3 and the ratio is 2. With 3 · 2^n, term 1 would be 6, not 3. The last choice adds instead of multiplying.

say.text: Big idea time. Linear growth adds the same amount over equal steps. Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor over equal steps.

show.text: Linear: equal differences (add) | Exponential: equal factors (multiply)

say.text: So with a table, run two tests. Subtract neighbors to get differences. Divide neighbors to get ratios. The x-values must be evenly spaced.

show.text: Same differences → linear | Same ratios → exponential | Example y: 3, 7, 11, 15 (+4 each) is linear | Example y: 3, 6, 12, 24 (×2 each) is exponential

say.text: Try it. The x-values go 0, 1, 2, 3 and the y-values are 2, 6, 18, 54.

ask.q: Is the table for y = 2, 6, 18, 54 linear or exponential?
ask.right: Exponential, because the ratios are all 3
wrong: Linear, because the numbers go up
Linear, because the differences are all 4
Exponential, because the differences are all 3
ask.why: The differences are 4, 12 and 36, which are not equal. The ratios are 3, 3 and 3, which are equal.

say.text: One more table. Run both tests again.

ask.q: Is the table for y = 7, 11, 15, 19 linear or exponential?
ask.right: Linear, because the differences are all 4
wrong: Exponential, because the numbers keep growing
Exponential, because the ratios are all 4
Linear, because the ratios are all 2
ask.why: Each step adds 4, so the differences are equal. The ratios (11÷7, 15÷11, 19÷15) are not equal.

say.text: Stories give hints too. A fixed amount each step means linear. Doubling, tripling, or a percent each step means exponential.

show.text:
Adds $5 each week → linear
Doubles every day → exponential
Grows 10% each year → exponential

say.text: Check yourself with a story.

ask.right: A rumor spreads so the number of people who know it doubles every hour
wrong: A bus ticket costs $3 per ride
ask.why: Doubling means multiplying by the same factor each hour. The other three add or repeat a fixed amount.

say.text: Back to our two deals. Deal A is 10 coins per level. On a graph it is a straight line, because it adds the same amount each time.

show.text: Deal A: coins earned at each level (adds 10)

say.text: Deal B starts at 1 and doubles. On a graph it is a curve. It starts low, then bends sharply upward.

show.text: Deal B: coins earned at each level (doubles)

ask.q: A graph starts low and then curves steeply upward. Which kind of growth is it most likely?
ask.why: Linear growth makes a straight line. A curve that bends steeply upward is the shape of exponential growth.

say.text: At first Deal A looks better: 10 coins beats 1. But exponential growth eventually passes linear growth. Compare the two charts level by level.

show.text: Level 7: A = 70, B = 64 | Level 8: A = 80, B = 128

ask.q: At which level does Deal B first earn more coins than Deal A?
ask.why: At level 7, B has 64 and A has 70, so A is still ahead. At level 8, B has 128 and A has 80, so B takes the lead.

say.text: Nice work, {name}. Recap: a geometric sequence multiplies by a common ratio. Its rule is aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1). Equal differences mean linear. Equal ratios mean exponential.

show.text:
Common ratio = term ÷ previous term
Rule: aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1)
Equal differences → linear
Equal ratios → exponential
Exponential eventually passes linear

other_side.claim: The explicit rule for a geometric sequence is aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1).
other_side.other_view: This is not the only form. Textbooks often count from zero in real-life problems and write aₙ = a₀ · rⁿ, where the first value is at n = 0. Both describe the same pattern. Check whether your problem starts counting at 0 or at 1.
